newsitem.title: USA: Rubin says Japanese seem committed to growth.
newsitem.headline: Rubin says Japanese seem committed to growth.

text.p: U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said Saturday that the Japanese seem committed to policies to keep growth going in their country.

Speaking at a press briefing following a meeting of the Group of Seven industrial countries, Rubin said, "I certainly came away satisfied ... They are very focused on the importance of having an appropriate mix of fiscal and monetary policies to maintain growth."
Rubin also made clear that the G7 economic leadership was in favor of the debt initiative to help heavily indebted poor countries reduce some of their burden.

He said the group considered the initiative so important that it agreed to put aside the divisive issue of whether the International Monetary Fund should sell a part of its gold to help finance the plan to a later time.
"We agreed to get going and leave the gold issue for resolution further down the road," Rubin said.

The Treasury secretary said that in his discussions with the European ministers he came away with the impression that they were committed to achieving the EMU and were making progress in that direction.
"It would be fair to say there was a general expression that they were moving toward an EMU," he said, adding that progress was being made in achieving the goal.
Asked specifically whether there was any discussion about the impact of the EMU on the U.S. dollar, Rubin said the G7 "never got into the impact on the dollar."

Asked about a plan to have a new allocation of the IMF's own money, the special drawing right, for countries that recently joined the international agency and had missed previous allocations, Rubin said the G7 was in favor of such an equity issue.
But he seemed to make clear that the 26 billion SDR level being proposed by IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus required further negotiation.
"I think it would be fair to say that that is an issue that is yet unresolved," he said.
Rubin was also asked about a statement by World Bank President James Wolfensohn that the first debt initiative cases could occur before the end of year.
He said he was not familiar with the statement but hoped that quick agreement could be reached in upcoming meetings and the program could move forward promptly.
"Our hope would be to move very quickly," Rubin said.
